title: The happiness of Hazelbrook
summary: The happiness of Hazelbrook by Charlotte Grace O'Brien is a didactic Christian domestic novella from the Victorian era. It centers on village life and the moral themes of duty before pleasure, repentance, and compassionate charity, showing how faith and steadfast goodness shape a family and their neighbors. Widow Lawrence struggles to raise her children, including industrious Ben, lively Katie, and bedridden Nelly. Tempted by idle friends, Katie slips into disobedience, sneaks to a fair, and is nearly killed in a thunderstorm, which leads to confession and reform. A smallpox outbreak following the fair claims two wayward youths and humbles Fanny Price, who recovers changed for the better. Gentle Mabel Tracy from the local manor brings comfort, Scripture, and an allegory of salvation that steadies hearts. A parallel thread follows blind Granny Hale, whose long-lost son Tom, broken by years at sea and brought to repentance, returns and becomes a faithful support. Nelly dies peacefully, trusting in Christ; Katie grows dutiful, declines a promising position to help her mother, later marries the reformed Tom, and they build a happy, orderly home—underscoring the book’s message that obedience, humility, and grace bring true happiness.
